top_choice_rationale: P001 (Autor, Hanson, Katz) best meets the common criteria. It pairs a conceptual account of skill demand and tasks with design-based local-labour-market evidence on how technology and trade shift labour demand and where adjustment costs fall. The work is mature, with roughly three decades of skill-premium research and over a decade of trade-shock papers, and it has been replicated, extended across countries and strongly criticised. The live disputes concern the magnitude and persistence of effects, not whether they exist, and the citation can avoid claiming either. Attribution is the weak point. Katz's marginal credit overlaps with the Goldin work, and Dorn is excluded by the three-name cap. I still rank P001 above P002 because Katz's wage-structure and skill-premium line supplies the framework that makes the trade evidence a statement about labour demand, not only local adjustment. This is a close judgment, and the citation should rest Katz on that line and not on the education-technology work with Goldin. P002 is a coherent, cleaner trade-shock prize with a defensible credit map, so I rank it second and well above no award. P000 is last because the achievement is mature, well replicated and prize-worthy under either trio.
recusal_note: No personal, institutional or co-authorship tie to Autor, Hanson, Katz or Dorn is apparent from my profile. I disclose field proximity: my work on electrification, railroads, labour conflict and regional adjustment is topically adjacent to B006, and I have applied the common criteria. I am a Lund colleague of Tommy Andersson, who is not a candidate, and Jan Teorell was formerly at Lund. I note this without adjudicating it.
